However, the 'pool4' subset (top 4 recent performers: ARIMA, THETA, rf, ONLY_DWT_catboost) yielded a better RMSE in attempt a1. I will now test a robust combination on this specific high-performing subset to see if narrowing the pool while maintaining robustness improves the score further.

The series has unstable rankings but strong trend/seasonality components captured by different model families. To test robustness against the specific correlation groups identified (linear/THETA family vs tree-based family), I will test a DBA (Dynamic Bootstrap Aggregation) on the full pool, which can handle correlated errors better than simple mean or fixed weights by resampling models.

The leader `a2` (simple mean) has a narrow margin. Testing `softmax_neg_error` weights will check if emphasizing top performers helps, though with unstable rankings, this risks overfitting to recent noise compared to robust averaging.

The leader `a2` (simple mean of all 19 models) has a marginally better score than weighted strategies, but the gap is indistinguishable. Given the "unstable" ranking and "low" predictability, robustness is key. However, simple mean may be diluted by weaker models. I will test a trimmed mean on the full pool to reduce the impact of potential outliers in the model forecasts, which might help given the high spectral entropy (noise-like behavior).
Median of top 4 models from window 2, focusing on independent error sources.

The current leader (a2) is a simple mean over all 19 models. While robust, it dilutes signal with noise given the low predictability and unstable ranking. I will test a trimmed mean on the full pool to remove the worst-performing tail without discarding potentially complementary models entirely, leveraging the 'robust' hint for noisy series.
Test if inverse error weighting on the top 4 diverse models improves over their simple mean (a1) or global mean (a2).

The current leader (mean on full pool) benefits from broad diversification which is valuable given the unstable ranking (ranking_tau=0.088) and low predictability. To test if a more robust combination method can leverage this diversity better than simple averaging, I will try DBA (Distribution-Based Averaging) on the top 4 models, which represents a different aggregation logic than mean/median/trimmed_mean already tested.
